title: 10. Exercises: Memory Management Masterclass (Part 1)
objectives: Solve the Memory Management Masterclass exercises without looking at the lesson
Test edge cases and explain your approach

sections.title: How Python Memory Works (Big Picture) — Coding Challenges — Concept 01
sections.body:
```
CHALLENGE 1:
Write a function demonstrate_references() that:
  a) Creates an integer, list, and dictionary
  b) Prints the id() of each
  c) Creates a second variable pointing to each
  d) Shows they share the same id (same object)
  e) Reassigns one variable and shows the id changes

CHALLENGE 2:
Write a memory_size_explorer() that:
  a) Creates objects of each type: int, float, str, list, tuple, dict, set, bool
  b) Uses sys.getsizeof() to print the size of each
  c) Shows how the size grows as you add elements to list/dict
  d) Explains (in comments) WHY each has the size it does

CHALLENGE 3:
Write a reference_count_tracker() that:
  a) Creates an object and prints its refcount (sys.getrefcount)
  b) Adds it to a list and shows refcount increases
  c) Passes it to a function and shows refcount increases inside
  d) Assigns to multiple variables and tracks refcount
  e) Uses del to remove references and shows refcount decreasing
  (Remember: getrefcount adds 1 temporary reference)

CHALLENGE 4:
Build a memory_layer_demo() that uses tracemalloc to:
  a) Measure memory BEFORE creating a large data structure
  b) Create a list of 100,000 integers
  c) Measure memory AFTER creation
  d) Delete the list
  e) Measure memory AFTER deletion
  f) Print how much memory was used and reclaimed

CHALLENGE 5:
Write an object_model_inspector(obj) that takes any object and prints:
  a) Its type (type())
  b) Its id (id())
  c) Its memory address in hex (hex(id()))
  d) Its size in bytes (sys.getsizeof())
  e) Its reference count (sys.getrefcount() - 1)
  f) Whether it's mutable or immutable (try/except approach)
  Test with: int, str, list, dict, tuple, custom class

CHALLENGE 6:
Demonstrate the "pass by object reference" behavior:
  a) Write a function that tries to rebind its parameter
     (show it does NOT affect the caller)
  b) Write a function that mutates its parameter
     (show it DOES affect the caller)
  c) Write a function that shows the id before/during/after
  d) Write a function that handles both mutable and immutable correctly
  e) Write a function that creates a safe copy before mutating

CHALLENGE 7:
Build a mini memory monitor using tracemalloc:
  a) Start tracing
  b) Run several operations (create lists, dicts, strings)
  c) Take a snapshot every 5 operations
  d) Compare snapshots to show which operations use most memory
  e) Stop tracing and print a final report
  f) Show top 5 memory-consuming lines in your code
```

sections.title: Stack Memory vs Heap Memory — Coding Challenges — Concept 02
sections.body:
```
CHALLENGE 1:
Write a call_stack_visualizer() function that:
  a) Uses inspect.stack() to get the current call stack
  b) Prints each frame with function name, line number, and local variables
  c) Shows the stack depth at each level
  d) Call it from 3 levels of nested functions to see the full stack
  e) Compare stack depth with/without recursive calls

CHALLENGE 2:
Demonstrate stack frame creation and destruction:
  a) Write a function that prints its frame id (id(sys._getframe()))
  b) Show that each call creates a new frame (different id)
  c) Show that the frame is destroyed after return
  d) Show that heap objects survive after their creating frame dies
  e) Capture the id of a heap object created in a function,
     then verify it's the same id after the function returns

CHALLENGE 3:
Recursion vs Iteration memory comparison:
  a) Implement factorial RECURSIVELY
  b) Implement factorial ITERATIVELY
  c) Use tracemalloc to measure memory for n=500 for both
  d) Use sys.getrecursionlimit() and try n=1500 recursively
  e) Handle RecursionError gracefully
  f) Show that iterative is both safer AND uses less memory

CHALLENGE 4:
Build a stack overflow protector:
  a) Write a recursive function that tracks current depth
  b) If depth > 800 (safe threshold below 1000 limit),
     raise a custom StackOverflowWarning
  c) Use try/except to catch it gracefully
  d) Automatically convert to iterative if recursion is too deep
  e) Test with a tree traversal function on a tree of depth 1500

CHALLENGE 5:
Heap object lifetime experiment:
  a) Create an object in a function
  b) Print its id inside the function
  c) Return the object to the caller
  d) Verify same id in caller (heap object survived)
  e) Delete the caller's reference
  f) Try to detect that the object was freed (use gc callbacks)
  g) Create a new object and check if Python reuses the same address

CHALLENGE 6:
Closure memory demonstration:
  a) Create a closure that captures a large list (100,000 items)
  b) Delete the outer function's local reference
  c) Show the list is STILL alive (closure keeps it alive)
  d) Measure memory before and after creating the closure
  e) Delete the closure and show memory is reclaimed
  f) Demonstrate a closure memory leak scenario and its fix

CHALLENGE 7:
Build a recursive call depth tracker:
  a) Create a decorator @track_stack_depth
  b) It should track maximum stack depth seen for any function
  c) It should warn if depth exceeds 50% of recursion limit
  d) It should provide a report: max_depth, calls_made, avg_depth
  e) Apply it to a recursive Fibonacci function
  f) Apply it to a recursive binary search
  g) Compare the depth profiles of both algorithms
```

sections.title: Python Objects & Memory Allocation — Coding Challenges — Concept 03
sections.body:
```
CHALLENGE 1:
Object size explorer:
  a) Create objects of every major Python type
  b) Print the size using sys.getsizeof() for each
  c) Show how size grows as you add elements to containers
  d) Calculate: at what number of elements does a list
     surpass a tuple's size?
  e) Graph the growth (text-based bar chart)

CHALLENGE 2:
List growth pattern analyzer:
  a) Create an empty list
  b) Append items one by one from 0 to 100
  c) After EACH append, record: item_count, sys.getsizeof()
  d) Print when the list REALLOCATES (size changes)
  e) Calculate the growth factor for each reallocation
  f) Estimate the over-allocation % at each step

CHALLENGE 3:
Deep size calculator:
  Write a function total_size(obj) that:
  a) Calculates the COMPLETE memory of an object including
     all objects it references (recursively)
  b) Handles cycles (use seen set with id())
  c) Works for: int, str, list, dict, tuple, set, custom classes
  d) Test with a nested dict structure 3 levels deep
  e) Compare with sys.getsizeof() to show the difference

CHALLENGE 4:
Memory-efficient record storage experiment:
  Store 100,000 user records using 5 different approaches:
  a) List of dicts
  b) List of tuples
  c) List of namedtuples
  d) List of dataclasses (with __slots__)
  e) NumPy structured array
  Measure total memory for each, print comparison table,
  declare a winner for memory efficiency.

CHALLENGE 5:
Object creation performance benchmark:
  Benchmark object creation for 1M iterations:
  a) Create 1M integers via: list(range(1M))
  b) Create 1M strings via: [str(i) for i in range(1M)]
  c) Create 1M tuples via: [(i, i*2) for i in range(1M)]
  d) Create 1M dicts via: [{'k': i} for i in range(1M)]
  Measure: time to create + peak memory usage
  Calculate: objects per second for each type

CHALLENGE 6:
PyMalloc pool visualization:
  Write code that demonstrates pool reuse:
  a) Create 1000 small objects (< 512 bytes)
  b) Record their ids
  c) Delete all of them
  d) Create 1000 new objects of same type
  e) Check if any new objects got the same id as old ones
     (shows memory block reuse from pymalloc pool)
  f) Do the same with large objects (> 512 bytes)
  g) Compare reuse rates between small and large objects

CHALLENGE 7:
Production memory profiler:
  Build a decorator @profile_memory that:
  a) Measures memory before and after function execution
  b) Reports: peak memory used, net memory change
  c) Reports: number of new objects created (using gc.get_objects())
  d) Warns if function uses > 100MB
  e) Optionally forces garbage collection before measurement
  Apply to 3 different functions with different memory profiles:
  - A function creating many small objects
  - A function creating few large objects
  - A function that creates then frees objects
```

sections.title: Mutable vs Immutable Objects in Memory — Coding Challenges — Concept 04
sections.body:
```
CHALLENGE 1:
Mutability identifier:
  Write a function is_mutable(obj) that:
  a) Returns True if the object is mutable, False if immutable
  b) Uses try/except with hash() to determine this
  c) Test with: int, str, float, list, dict, set, tuple,
     frozenset, bytes, bytearray, custom class
  d) Print a summary table of all Python built-in types

CHALLENGE 2:
String concatenation performance:
  Build a string of 50,000 items using FIVE different methods:
  a) result = '' then result += item in loop
  b) ''.join(list_of_items)
  c) io.StringIO buffer
  d) f-string in loop (result = f'{result}{item}')
  e) functools.reduce with operator.add
  Measure time AND peak memory for each.
  Plot results as a text-based bar chart.

CHALLENGE 3:
Aliasing bug detector:
  Write a function detect_aliasing(obj1, obj2) that:
  a) Returns True if obj1 and obj2 share any mutable sub-objects
  b) Works for lists of lists, dicts with list values, etc.
  c) Uses id() comparison to detect shared references
  d) Test with:
     - Two shallow copies of a nested list
     - Two deep copies of a nested list
     - Original and its alias

CHALLENGE 4:
Safe copy patterns:
  Demonstrate all copy patterns and their memory implications:
  a) Assignment (alias): no copy, same object
  b) Slice copy (lst[:]): shallow copy
  c) list() constructor: shallow copy
  d) copy.copy(): shallow copy
  e) copy.deepcopy(): deep copy
  For each, show: id() comparison, mutation test,
  and memory usage (tracemalloc)

CHALLENGE 5:
Mutable default argument fixer:
  Find and fix the bugs in these functions:
  a) def add_tag(item, tags=[]): tags.append(item); return tags
  b) def init_config(config={}): config['debug'] = True; return config
  c) def make_matrix(rows=3, data=[[0]*3]*3): return data
  For each:
  - Demonstrate the bug (call twice, show problem)
  - Fix it properly
  - Verify the fix works correctly
  - Explain WHY the bug happens in memory terms

CHALLENGE 6:
Immutability performance experiment:
  Compare mutable vs immutable for:
  a) Building: list append vs tuple concatenation (100K items)
  b) Accessing: list[i] vs tuple[i] (1M accesses)
  c) Hashing: set of tuples vs dict with tuple keys (100K items)
  d) Memory: 1000 tuples vs 1000 lists of same content
  Measure time and memory for each pair.

CHALLENGE 7:
Build a copy-on-write wrapper:
  Implement a CopyOnWrite class that wraps a mutable list:
  a) Reading from it is fast (accesses original directly)
  b) Writing to it creates a private copy first (simulates CoW)
  c) Multiple CopyOnWrite objects can share the same underlying data
  d) The first write triggers a copy (and only then)
  e) Subsequent writes to the copy don't trigger another copy
  f) Use id() to prove sharing and copying behavior
  g) Measure memory savings when most objects are read-only
```

sections.title: Reference Counting (Core Mechanism) — Coding Challenges — Concept 05
sections.body:
```
CHALLENGE 1:
Build a RefCountTracker decorator:
  a) Wrap any function with @track_refcounts
  b) Before the call: record refcounts of all arguments
  c) During the call: sample refcounts at entry
  d) After the call: check refcounts of return value
  e) Detect if any argument's refcount is unexpectedly high
     (suggesting it's being held somewhere inside)
  f) Print a refcount lifecycle report for each call

CHALLENGE 2:
Reference leak detector:
  a) Write a function find_unexpected_references(obj) that:
  b) Uses gc.get_referrers(obj) to find all referrers
  c) Categorizes each referrer (dict, list, frame, module, etc.)
  d) Shows the name/key under which obj is stored
  e) Detects if any referrer is a global namespace
  f) Test with objects that are: in globals, in a closure,
     in a class attribute, and in an exception traceback

CHALLENGE 3:
Lifecycle event system using __del__:
  a) Build a Resource class that tracks creation/destruction
  b) Use class variable to count total alive instances
  c) Use __del__ to decrement count and log destruction
  d) Create 100 instances in a loop
  e) Verify all 100 are destroyed when loop ends
  f) Test with circular references (show some survive!)
  g) Use gc.collect() to clean up the survivors
  h) Verify all are eventually destroyed

CHALLENGE 4:
Refcount visualization tool:
  a) Create a RefcountMonitor class
  b) It should watch a specific object by id()
  c) Provide snapshot() method that records current refcount
  d) Provide history() method that shows refcount over time
  e) Use it to trace the lifecycle of a list through:
     - Creation
     - Multiple assignments
     - Container storage
     - Function calls
     - Deletion

CHALLENGE 5:
Prove the GIL protects refcounts:
  a) Create a shared integer object
  b) Spawn 10 threads, each making 100,000 references to it
  c) Verify final refcount is correct (all threads done + del'd refs)
  d) Measure time with threading vs multiprocessing
  e) Show that CPU-bound tasks don't benefit from threading
     (due to GIL) but I/O-bound tasks DO benefit

CHALLENGE 6:
Memory pool reuse demonstration:
  a) Create 1000 objects, record their ids
  b) Delete all 1000 objects
  c) Create 1000 new objects of SAME type
  d) Count how many new objects have the same id as old ones
     (proves pymalloc reuses freed blocks)
  e) Repeat with different types (int, str, list)
  f) Show that ids ARE reused for same-type, same-size objects

CHALLENGE 7:
Production reference audit tool:
  Build a complete audit tool that:
  a) Takes any object as input
  b) Finds ALL paths from GC roots to that object
     (uses gc.get_referrers() recursively)
  c) Prints each path as a chain: module → dict → list → obj
  d) Identifies which paths are 'expected' vs 'suspicious'
  e) Suggests fixes for suspicious references
     (e.g., "this is held in a global cache — use LRU")
  f) Works correctly without infinite loops (handle cycles)
```

sections.title: The id() Function & Object Identity — Coding Challenges — Concept 06
sections.body:
```
CHALLENGE 1:
Build an id() explorer:
  a) Create objects of 10 different types
  b) Print id() in both decimal and hex for each
  c) Show that each has a unique id
  d) Create two variables pointing to the same object
  e) Show they have the same id
  f) Rebind one variable and show ids diverge

CHALLENGE 2:
Integer cache boundary finder:
  a) Find the exact boundaries of Python's small integer cache
  b) Test every integer from -10 to 300
  c) For each, create two variables with that value
  d) Check if they share the same id
  e) Print a table showing: value, is_cached, id
  f) Verify the boundaries are exactly -5 to 256

CHALLENGE 3:
id() reuse experiment:
  a) Create and destroy 100 objects of the same type
  b) Record all ids used
  c) Count how many unique vs reused ids appeared
  d) Create all 100 objects SIMULTANEOUSLY (no del between)
  e) Show that no two live objects share an id
  f) Now delete them all and create 100 new ones
  g) Count id overlaps with the first batch

CHALLENGE 4:
Alias detector using id():
  Write a function find_aliases(namespace) that:
  a) Takes a dict (like globals() or locals())
  b) Groups variable names by the id() of their object
  c) Returns a dict: {id: [list_of_variable_names]}
  d) Only reports groups with 2+ names (actual aliases)
  e) Test by creating several aliases in a namespace
  f) Show: x = y = z = [1,2,3] creates 3 aliases

CHALLENGE 5:
Constant folding demonstration:
  a) Write two identical functions with same integer constants
  b) Use dis.dis() to inspect their bytecode
  c) Check if the constants have the same id()
  d) Compare: small integer (in cache) vs large integer
  e) Compare: script context vs eval() context
  f) Document your findings about when Python shares constants

CHALLENGE 6:
Safe unique ID system:
  Build a SafeID class that:
  a) Assigns a guaranteed-unique ID to any Python object
  b) ID persists even if object is moved/garbage collected
  c) Uses uuid4() for true uniqueness
  d) Provides a registry: SafeID.lookup(id_string) → object
  e) Uses WeakValueDictionary so objects can still be GC'd
  f) Test with objects that have the same Python id() (reuse)
  g) Prove your IDs are never confused even with address reuse

CHALLENGE 7:
Object graph visualizer using id():
  Build a visualize_object_graph(root) function that:
  a) Traverses all objects reachable from root
  b) Uses id() to track visited nodes (prevent infinite loops)
  c) Builds a graph: {id: {type, size, references_to: [ids]}}
  d) Detects and labels cycles
  e) Calculates total unique objects and total memory
  f) Prints a text-based tree representation
  g) Test with a nested dict, a circular linked list,
     and a class with back-references
```

sections.title: is vs == (Identity vs Equality) — Coding Challenges — Concept 07
sections.body:
```
CHALLENGE 1:
is vs == test suite:
  Write 20 test cases demonstrating when 'is' and '==' agree
  and when they differ. Cover:
  a) Small integers, large integers
  b) Short strings, long strings, computed strings
  c) None, True, False
  d) Empty containers vs None
  e) Custom objects with __eq__ overrides
  Print a table: expression | is result | == result | explanation

CHALLENGE 2:
None check performance benchmark:
  Compare 5 ways to check for None:
  a) x is None
  b) x == None
  c) not x  (WRONG for many cases — show why!)
  d) x is not None (positive check)
  e) type(x) is type(None)
  Benchmark each for 10M iterations.
  Identify which is fastest and which are semantically correct.

CHALLENGE 3:
Sentinel pattern implementation:
  Build a complete Sentinel class:
  a) Each sentinel instance is unique
  b) Has a descriptive name for debugging
  c) Cannot be equal to anything except itself
  d) Has a proper __repr__
  e) Use it in: get_config(key, default=MISSING) where None
     is a valid config value
  f) Test: passing None explicitly vs not passing a default

CHALLENGE 4:
Custom __eq__ exploration:
  Build 3 classes with different __eq__ behaviors:
  a) ValueEqual: equal if all attributes match
  b) AlwaysEqual: equal to everything
  c) IdEqual: equal only if same object (override to use 'is')
  For each, show what 'is' vs '==' gives.
  Show which can be used in sets, which as dict keys.

CHALLENGE 5:
Linter for is vs == mistakes:
  Write a code analyzer that:
  a) Takes a Python source file as input
  b) Finds all uses of 'is' with literals (numbers, strings)
  c) Finds all uses of '==' with None, True, False
  d) Reports each as a warning with line number
  e) Suggests the correct replacement
  Test on a file containing intentional mistakes.

CHALLENGE 6:
NaN identity puzzle:
  Explore NaN (Not a Number) behavior:
  a) Show nan == nan is False (IEEE 754)
  b) Show nan is nan can be True (same object) or True/False
  c) Show nan in [nan] is False (uses ==)
  d) Show {nan: 'value'}[nan] works (uses hash then ==)
  e) Show how to correctly check for NaN: math.isnan()
  f) Build a nan-safe comparison function
  g) Show set behavior with nan

CHALLENGE 7:
Production None safety checker:
  Build a decorator @none_safe that:
  a) Wraps a function and checks all arguments for None
  b) Uses 'is None' (not '== None') for the check
  c) Allows specifying which arguments can be None
  d) Raises TypeError with clear message for unexpected None
  e) Works with positional and keyword arguments
  f) Handles default arguments correctly
  g) Test with functions that have custom __eq__ arguments
```

sections.title: sys.getrefcount() — Counting References — Coding Challenges — Concept 08
sections.body:
```
CHALLENGE 1:
Build a refcount logger:
  a) Create a class RefCountLogger
  b) wrap(obj) method: starts tracking an object
  c) snapshot() method: records current refcount with timestamp
  d) report() method: prints refcount history over time
  e) Use it to track a dict through: creation, assignment,
     container storage, function calls, deletion

CHALLENGE 2:
Refcount-based leak detector:
  a) Build a function monitor_refcounts(objects_dict)
  b) Takes {name: object} and records their refcounts
  c) Run at regular intervals (simulate with loop)
  d) Alert when any object's refcount unexpectedly grows
  e) Test with an intentional leak (appending to global list)
  f) Verify the alert fires correctly

CHALLENGE 3:
Reference chain finder:
  a) Given an object with high refcount, find the full chain
  b) Start from gc.get_referrers(obj)
  c) For each referrer, find ITS referrers
  d) Stop when reaching module globals or frame
  e) Print the chain: frame.local → list → your_object
  f) Test with 3 levels of nested containers holding the object

CHALLENGE 4:
Closure reference analyzer:
  a) Create a function that creates closures
  b) Before creating closure: record refcount of captured var
  c) After creating closure: record refcount again
  d) Verify refcount increased by exactly 1 per closure
  e) Delete closures one by one, verify refcount decreases
  f) Create 100 closures capturing the same variable
  g) Verify total refcount increase = 100

CHALLENGE 5:
Context manager refcount verifier:
  Build a @verify_no_refcount_leak decorator:
  a) Measures refcount of all arguments before function call
  b) Measures refcount after function call
  c) Asserts refcount returned to baseline (no leak)
  d) Reports any unexpected refcount increases with gc.get_referrers
  e) Apply to functions that: use context managers,
     append to lists, use closures

CHALLENGE 6:
Container refcount experiment:
  For each container type (list, dict, tuple, set, deque):
  a) Add the same object to each container
  b) Record refcount after each addition
  c) Add the object multiple times to the same container
     (list allows duplicates, set doesn't)
  d) Record refcount for each duplicate
  e) Show: list [obj, obj] = +2, set {obj} = +1
  f) Delete containers and verify refcount returns to 1

CHALLENGE 7:
Production refcount audit framework:
  Build a complete audit system:
  a) AuditedObject: wrapper that tracks all reference events
  b) Hooks into Python's gc to detect new referrers
  c) Maintains a log: when ref was added, by whom, when removed
  d) Provides report: reference lifetime analysis
  e) Detects references that outlived their expected lifetime
  f) Test with: short-lived function references,
     long-lived global references,
     and unexpected closure captures
```

sections.title: Garbage Collector (gc module) — Coding Challenges — Concept 09
sections.body:
```
CHALLENGE 1:
GC basics exercise:
  a) Create 100 circular reference pairs (A→B, B→A)
  b) Delete all variable references
  c) Verify they're NOT freed by refcount (check gc.get_count())
  d) Call gc.collect() and verify they ARE freed
  e) Add gc callbacks to log when collection happens
  f) Print: objects before collect, objects collected, objects after

CHALLENGE 2:
Generation tracking:
  a) Create objects and track which generation they're in
  b) Use gc.get_count() to monitor gen0/gen1/gen2 counts
  c) Create 700+ new objects to trigger automatic gen0 collection
  d) Observe which objects survive to gen1
  e) Force gen2 collection and observe behavior
  f) Explain the generational hypothesis with your observations

CHALLENGE 3:
Memory leak finder using gc:
  a) Write a function that simulates a memory leak (circular refs)
  b) Write a leak_check() function that:
     - Takes a snapshot of gc.get_objects() before
     - Runs the leaky function
     - Forces gc.collect()
     - Compares snapshots
     - Reports new objects that survived GC (potential leaks)
  c) Fix the leak and verify leak_check() reports clean

CHALLENGE 4:
GC performance benchmark:
  a) Create a workload that creates 500K objects with NO cycles
  b) Create a similar workload WITH circular references (500K cycles)
  c) Measure time for both WITH GC enabled
  d) Measure time for both WITHOUT GC (gc.disable())
  e) Compare: GC overhead for cyclic vs non-cyclic workloads
  f) Find the sweet spot: when is disabling GC beneficial?

CHALLENGE 5:
gc.garbage investigator:
  a) In Python 3, create a scenario where gc.garbage might be populated
     (object's __del__ raises an exception during collection)
  b) Inspect gc.garbage contents
  c) Write a clear_garbage() function that safely drains gc.garbage
  d) Add a gc callback that logs to gc.garbage occurrences
  e) Document: when does gc.garbage get populated in Python 3.4+?

CHALLENGE 6:
Build a memory dashboard:
  Using gc module, build a real-time dashboard that:
  a) Shows current generation counts every second
  b) Shows top 5 object types by count
  c) Shows total tracked objects count
  d) Shows how many GC collections have occurred
  e) Alerts when gen2 count exceeds a threshold (too many long-lived cycles)
  f) Runs for 30 seconds then prints a summary report

CHALLENGE 7:
GC-aware object pool:
  Build an ObjectPool class that:
  a) Pre-creates N objects of a given type
  b) Lends objects to callers (checkout/checkin pattern)
  c) Tracks which objects are in use vs available
  d) Disables GC during bulk checkout operations
  e) Verifies no object leaks (all checked in eventually)
  f) Uses gc.get_referrers to detect if checked-out objects
     are accidentally stored in external caches
  g) Runs gc.collect() between checkout batches
```

sections.title: Cyclic / Circular References — Coding Challenges — Concept 10
sections.body:
```
CHALLENGE 1:
Cycle creator and detector:
  a) Create 5 different cycle patterns:
     - Self-referential dict
     - Two-node cycle
     - Three-node cycle (A→B→C→A)
     - List containing itself
     - Object with dict containing the object
  b) For each, verify refcount doesn't drop to 0 after del
  c) Use gc.collect() to free each
  d) Verify they're freed after gc.collect()
  e) Count objects freed for each pattern

CHALLENGE 2:
Tree implementation comparison:
  Build a binary tree node TWO ways:
  a) WITH cycles: parent has list of children,
     children have parent attribute (strong ref)
  b) WITHOUT cycles: children have parent attribute
     using weakref.ref()
  For each:
  - Build a tree of depth 10, width 2 (1023 nodes)
  - Delete the root
  - Measure: how many gc.collect() calls needed?
  - Measure: time to fully clean up
  - Verify all nodes are freed

CHALLENGE 3:
Observer pattern memory safety:
  Implement an EventEmitter class:
  a) Version 1: stores callbacks directly (leaks cycles)
  b) Version 2: stores weakref.WeakMethod callbacks (no leak)
  For each version:
  - Register 100 handlers from 100 different objects
  - Delete all handler objects
  - Check if event emitter still holds live references
  - Verify gc.garbage is empty
  - Measure memory before/after

CHALLENGE 4:
Cycle-safe linked list:
  Implement a doubly-linked list:
  a) Each node has next (strong) and prev (weak) references
  b) Test: inserting 1000 nodes
  c) Test: deleting from the middle (prev weak ref becomes None)
  d) Test: deleting the entire list (all freed immediately)
  e) Compare with naive implementation (both strong refs)
  f) Show: naive version requires gc.collect() for cleanup

CHALLENGE 5:
Django-style ORM cycle audit:
  Create a mini ORM with:
  a) Model class with ForeignKey relationships
  b) QuerySet that caches results
  c) Manager that holds references to model class
  Find all cycles created by this structure.
  Fix each cycle using appropriate technique:
  - weakref for back-references
  - IDs for cross-model references
  - __slots__ to prevent accidental attributes
  Verify: deleting a queryset frees all model instances

CHALLENGE 6:
Cycle statistics tracker:
  Build a tool that:
  a) Runs a given function 100 times
  b) After each run, counts gc-tracked objects
  c) Runs gc.collect() and counts again
  d) Reports: objects freed by refcount vs by GC
  e) Calculates: cycle rate (% objects needing GC vs refcount)
  f) Identifies which function creates the most cycles
  Test with 3 functions: no cycles, few cycles, many cycles

CHALLENGE 7:
Production cycle prevention framework:
  Build a NoCycles metaclass that:
  a) Intercepts __setattr__ on all instances
  b) When an attribute is set to an object, checks if
     that would create a cycle (using gc.get_referents traversal)
  c) If a cycle would be created, automatically converts
     the reference to a weakref
  d) Provides a property accessor that dereferences the weakref
  e) Logs all auto-converted references for debugging
  f) Test with: tree nodes, observer callbacks, parent-child
```

sections.title: Generational Garbage Collection — Coding Challenges — Concept 11
sections.body:
```
CHALLENGE 1:
Generation counter observer:
  a) Set gc callbacks to log every collection event
  b) Record: which generation, how many collected, timestamp
  c) Create workloads that trigger gen0, gen1, gen2 collections
  d) Plot a text timeline of collection events
  e) Calculate: average objects per collection per generation
  f) Identify the collection frequency ratio (gen0:gen1:gen2)

CHALLENGE 2:
Threshold tuning experiment:
  For 5 different threshold settings (very aggressive to very lenient):
  a) Run a standardized workload (50K object creates/deletes)
  b) Record: total time, peak memory, number of collections
  c) Plot the trade-off between memory and CPU
  d) Find the optimal threshold for: memory-sensitive mode,
     throughput-sensitive mode, and latency-sensitive mode
  e) Document your recommendation with data

CHALLENGE 3:
Generational promotion tracker:
  Build a system that tracks when specific objects are promoted:
  a) Create 100 named objects
  b) Force gen0 collection and detect which survived
  c) Force gen1 collection and detect which survived to gen2
  d) Show the "survival rate" at each generation
  e) Create objects designed to die young (no external refs)
     vs objects designed to survive (stored in list)
  f) Verify dying-young objects never reach gen1

CHALLENGE 4:
gc.freeze() performance test:
  a) Simulate app startup: load 10MB of config/model data
  b) WITHOUT freeze: measure per-request GC scan overhead
  c) WITH freeze: call gc.freeze() after startup, measure again
  d) Compare: collection time, objects scanned per collection
  e) Calculate memory savings from freeze in forked processes
  f) Show gc.get_freeze_count() vs gc.get_count()

CHALLENGE 5:
Real-time GC monitor:
  Build a monitoring daemon that:
  a) Runs in a background thread
  b) Every 100ms samples gc.get_count() and gc.get_stats()
  c) Detects when gen2 count exceeds threshold (leak warning)
  d) Records peak memory (tracemalloc)
  e) Prints a rolling report every 5 seconds
  f) Provides a summary: total collections, avg pause estimate

CHALLENGE 6:
Instagram-style request handler:
  Implement a mini web server class that:
  a) Freezes all objects after __init__
  b) Disables GC before handling requests
  c) Processes 10,000 simulated requests
  d) After every 100 requests, collects gen0 only
  e) After every 1000 requests, does a full collect
  f) Measures P50, P95, P99, max latency
  g) Compare with a version that uses default GC behavior

CHALLENGE 7:
Generation-aware object pool:
  Design an object pool that uses generational behavior:
  a) Pool keeps 'hot' objects in gen0 (recently used)
  b) Objects not used for a while naturally promote to gen1/gen2
  c) Pool can detect which objects are in which generation
     (using gc.get_count() before/after creating objects)
  d) Eviction policy: gen2 objects are evicted first
  e) Test with 1000 objects, varying access patterns
  f) Show memory usage vs naive pool implementation
```

sections.title: __del__ Method (Finalizers / Destructors) — Coding Challenges — Concept 12
sections.body:
```
CHALLENGE 1:
__del__ timing experiment:
  a) Create a class with __del__ that logs timestamp
  b) Test __del__ timing for: immediate del (refcount→0),
     del with other references alive, cyclic references
  c) Show: immediate del fires __del__ instantly
  d) Show: cyclic del requires gc.collect()
  e) Measure time between del and __del__ for each case

CHALLENGE 2:
__del__ vs context manager comparison:
  Build a resource class TWICE:
  a) Version 1: cleanup via __del__ only
  b) Version 2: cleanup via __exit__ + __del__ safety net
  For each, test:
  - Normal execution (cleanup happens)
  - Exception mid-use (cleanup must happen)
  - Object in a cycle (cleanup delay?)
  - Interpreter shutdown scenario (atexit handler test)
  Show which version is more reliable

CHALLENGE 3:
weakref.finalize complete implementation:
  Build a ConnectionPool using weakref.finalize:
  a) Pool tracks all connections via WeakValueDictionary
  b) Each connection registers a finalize callback
  c) Finalize callback returns connection to pool
  d) Pool can report: active, available, finalized counts
  e) Test: connections returned explicitly vs via GC
  f) Verify: no memory leaks, no double-returns

CHALLENGE 4:
Object resurrection experiment:
  a) Create a class whose __del__ resurrects itself
  b) Demonstrate the resurrection works (refcount goes 0→1→0)
  c) Show Python only calls __del__ ONCE even after resurrection
  d) Show the object IS eventually freed
  e) Demonstrate a USEFUL (but rare) resurrection pattern:
     returning a pooled object to a pool from __del__
  f) Show why this is fragile and what to use instead

CHALLENGE 5:
__del__ exception safety:
  a) Create a __del__ that raises an exception
  b) Show the exception goes to stderr (not propagated)
  c) Show the object IS still freed despite the exception
  d) Create a __del__ that conditionally raises
  e) Build a safe __del__ wrapper that:
     - Catches all exceptions
     - Logs them properly (to a logger, not print)
     - Ensures cleanup still happens
  f) Test with multiple cleanup steps that could fail

CHALLENGE 6:
Interpreter shutdown safety:
  Create a class that works correctly during shutdown:
  a) __del__ accesses module-level variables (the bug)
  b) Show it fails during interpreter exit
  c) Fix it by checking if globals are None
  d) Show weakref.finalize handles shutdown correctly
  e) Use atexit.register() as another alternative
  f) Document which approach works in which scenario

CHALLENGE 7:
Production resource manager:
  Build a complete ResourceManager class:
  a) Manages any type of resource (file, connection, lock)
  b) Tracks all resources: open, closed, leaked
  c) Uses weakref.finalize for safety net cleanup
  d) Provides context manager interface
  e) Reports leaked resources at program exit (using atexit)
  f) Measures time-to-cleanup for each resource
  g) Generates a cleanup report:
     - Resources properly closed
     - Resources closed by GC (warnings)
     - Resources leaked at exit (errors)
```

sections.title: Object Interning (String & Integer) — Coding Challenges — Concept 14

sections.title: Generators vs Lists (Memory Efficiency) — Coding Challenges — Concept 16

```
  b) Implement using generator approach
```

```
     at module level

CHALLENGE 2:
Closure memory measurement:
  a) Create a closure that captures a 1MB list
  b) Measure: list refcount with and without the closure
  c) Show: deleting the outer function variable doesn't free the list
  d) Show: deleting the closure DOES free the list
  e) Create 100 closures all capturing the same variable
  f) Measure refcount growth and memory usage

CHALLENGE 3:
Loop variable capture fix:
  Demonstrate 5 different ways to fix the loop capture bug:
  a) Default argument: lambda x=i: x
  b) Factory function: def make(i): return lambda: i
  c) functools.partial
  d) class with __call__
  e) list comprehension trick
  For each: show it's fixed (correct values), measure memory overhead

CHALLENGE 4:
Scope isolation testing:
  Build a test framework that:
  a) Runs a function in a completely isolated namespace
  b) Captures all global modifications made by the function
  c) Restores globals to original state after test
  d) Reports: new names added, names modified, names deleted
  e) Test with functions that accidentally modify globals

CHALLENGE 5:
Variable lifetime analyzer:
  Build a LifetimeTracker that:
  a) Intercepts object creation and destruction via gc callbacks
  b) Tracks: where was the object created (file, line, scope)
  c) Tracks: when it was destroyed (scope exit, explicit del, GC)
  d) Calculates: average lifetime per scope type (local vs global)
  e) Reports: top 10 longest-lived objects

CHALLENGE 6:
Memory-efficient counter using closure:
  Build a thread-safe counter system:
  a) make_counter(initial=0) returns (increment, decrement, get)
  b) Uses closures (nonlocal) for state
  c) Thread-safe using threading.Lock in the closure
  d) Supports reset, get_history (list of all values)
  e) Compare memory: closure approach vs class approach vs dict approach
  f) Benchmark: 1M increment operations for each approach

CHALLENGE 7:
Scope-aware memoize decorator:
  Build @scope_memoize decorator that:
  a) Caches function results in the CALLER's scope
     (not module-level — cache is cleaned up with the caller)
  b) Uses weakref to the calling frame to detect scope exit
  c) When caller scope exits, cache is automatically cleared
  d) Works for: regular functions, methods, nested functions
  e) Benchmark: compare with functools.lru_cache
  f) Show: scope_memoize doesn't leak between request handlers
     (unlike module-level lru_cache)
```

sections.title: Memory Leaks in Python — Coding Challenges — Concept 20
sections.body:
```
CHALLENGE 1:
Leak pattern detector:
  Write a function that analyzes a Python source file and flags:
  a) Module-level mutable collections (dict, list, set)
     that appear to grow in functions (append, update, etc.)
  b) Class-level mutable defaults
  c) Stored exception variables (except X as e: store(e))
  d) Functions that register callbacks without weakref
  e) Thread-local data set without corresponding cleanup
  Output: file:line warnings with explanation

CHALLENGE 2:
tracemalloc leak harness:
  Build a @detect_leak decorator that:
  a) Runs the decorated function N times
  b) Takes tracemalloc snapshots before and after
  c) Compares snapshots to find growing allocations
  d) Reports: bytes leaked per call, top allocation sites
  e) Raises AssertionError if growth exceeds threshold
  f) Test with: known leaky function, known clean function

CHALLENGE 3:
Object count monitor:
  Build a tool that monitors object counts by type over time:
  a) Sample gc.get_objects() every second
  b) Track growth of each type
  c) Alert when any type grows > 10% per second
  d) Show a rolling 60-second window
  e) Simulate a leak (append to global list in background thread)
  f) Verify: alert fires correctly, stops when leak is fixed

CHALLENGE 4:
Exception leak reproducer and fixer:
  a) Create a 10-level deep call stack
  b) Raise and catch an exception at the bottom
  c) Measure memory of stored exception (full traceback)
  d) Verify: locals of each frame are held alive
  e) Apply all three fixes: str(e), e.__traceback__=None, format_exc()
  f) Measure memory for each fix
  g) Show: each fix reduces memory proportionally to call depth

CHALLENGE 5:
Cache leak comparison:
  Compare 5 cache implementations for leak safety:
  a) Plain dict (leaks forever)
  b) dict with manual eviction (bounded, manual effort)
  c) functools.lru_cache (bounded, automatic)
  d) WeakValueDictionary (evicts when values are GC'd)
  e) cachetools.TTLCache (time-based eviction)
  For each: run 10K requests, measure memory growth
  Plot: memory vs requests for each approach

CHALLENGE 6:
Production leak simulation and fix:
  Build a mini web service with 3 intentional leaks:
  a) Leak 1: request logger storing full request objects
  b) Leak 2: signal/callback system with strong refs
  c) Leak 3: user session cache that never evicts
  For each:
  - Run 1000 simulated requests
  - Measure memory growth
  - Apply the fix
  - Verify memory is now stable

CHALLENGE 7:
Memory regression test suite:
  Build a complete memory regression testing framework:
  a) define_baseline(func, args): runs func, records memory profile
  b) assert_stable(func, args, runs=100): verifies func doesn't leak
  c) compare_implementations(funcs, args): finds the most memory-efficient
  d) generate_report(): produces HTML/text report with:
     - Per-function memory growth charts
     - Top allocation sites
     - Pass/fail status
     - Recommendations
  e) Integrate with pytest: @memory_stable decorator
```
